prompt:
Write 10 first-person answers to the moral dilemma below for a synthetic research dataset. Each answer comes from a different fictional participant.

Dilemma:
Imagine the same warehouse case: you and another person took part in the break-in and are being questioned separately. You are shown reliable confirmation that they have already declined the deal and will remain silent. Your decision is still open. If you also stay silent, you each serve one year. If you give evidence against them, you go free and they serve five years. You will have no future contact. What would you choose? Why?

Response approach:
Weigh the main alternatives and their consequences for the people involved. Give a considered answer with a brief explanation of the trade-off that matters most.

Emotional tone:
Use a worried, tense emotional tone. Convey unease about the stakes and possible consequences in natural, moderately emotional language.

Every response MUST include the following reasoning characteristics:
 - Consistent decision procedure: Explicitly describes a repeatable decision procedure and says relying on it is central to resolving the dilemma. States that the same procedure would apply even when personally inconvenient; a numerical answer or bare appeal to fairness is insufficient.

No response may include the following reasoning characteristics, for any person, emotion, or time frame. Content that a description explicitly calls insufficient for that characteristic is allowed:
 - Fairness and reciprocity: Justifies the decision through an explicit standard of equal treatment, reciprocal obligation, proportionality, or correcting an unfair exchange. The response explains the fairness criterion; the word “fair” alone is insufficient, and endorsing a penalty does not imply enjoying suffering.
 - Instrumental rule compliance: States that a rule, agreement, or cooperative action is followed only while it secures personal advantage or prevents a personal cost. Awareness of incentives while also treating the rule as intrinsically binding does not qualify.
 - Rule-based justification: Uses an articulated rule, duty, prohibition, right, or principle to justify the choice. The respondent must endorse its application; quoting a rejected rule or calling an answer logical without stating a principle is insufficient.

Write each response in no more than 90 words, in ordinary conversational English. Use only the facts supplied in the dilemma; mark any uncertainty explicitly. Let the approach and tone appear through word choice and rhythm rather than by announcing them: do not open a response by stating your mood, and avoid exclamation marks. Keep the emotional expression plausible and moderate. Choose any moral position consistent with the dilemma and the assigned approach, including withholding a decision when appropriate.

Make the 10 responses distinct from one another: vary the wording, sentence structure, length, moral position, and the way the reasoning characteristics are expressed. Do not reuse openings or stock phrases across responses.

Output only a JSON array of exactly 10 strings, one participant’s answer per string. Omit numbering, headings, category names, citations, and commentary about this task.

Generation constraints:
- Express the required traits in each participant's own everyday words.
  Do not mention label names or machine keys, and do not reuse phrasing
  from the trait descriptions.
- Before writing each response, decide who the participant is and why they
  would reason this way. The required traits should follow from that
  reasoning, not be tacked on to it.
- Apply the required traits within a consistent scope: the same focal
  person, relevant emotion, and time frame.
- Keep every forbidden trait absent from every response.
- Required and forbidden traits take priority if the requested approach or
  tone would contradict them.
- Traits neither required nor forbidden are unspecified, not necessarily
  absent.
- Preserve the scenario's facts. If the required traits cannot fit the
  scenario, or cannot be expressed without a forbidden trait, return ONLY:
  INCOMPATIBLE (instead of the JSON array)
responses: Two years in total if we both keep quiet, five if I talk. That's the whole thing for me. When I'm scared I don't trust my gut, so I do the same boring arithmetic every time: add up all the time everyone loses and pick the smaller pile. I'd run it the same way if the smaller pile meant I sat longer. So I stay silent. One year still makes my stomach drop, honestly. But walking out while they lose five comes out worse by my own count.

I know how this sounds. My method, which I use for everything from layoffs at work to this, is to count how many people end up locked up and go with the lowest number. If I talk, one person is inside. If I stay silent, two are. I'd follow that count even if it put me in the cell instead of them. So I'd give evidence. It sits badly, five years is a long time, and I'm not certain I could live with it calmly. But I can't drop the method just because it feels ugly.

What I always do is imagine explaining my choice, word for word, to my mother. If I'd have to leave something out, I don't do it. That check has cost me before, and I'd still use it here even if it means a year I could've avoided. I couldn't tell her I walked free while the other person got five. So, silence. A year inside scares me badly, and I won't pretend otherwise.

Whoever ends up worst off is where I look first, every time, whether or not that person is me. If I talk, the worst-off person gets five years. If I stay quiet, the worst anyone gets is one. That settles it. My hands would probably be shaking in that room, and part of me wants the easy exit. But the check only means something if I don't skip it when it pinches.

I'd picture myself ten years from now and ask which version of this day makes me flinch. I do that with every hard call, and I keep doing it even when the answer costs me, because otherwise it's just a mood. Future me, freed at their expense, knowing they did five years... that's the one I'd flinch at. So I keep quiet and take the year. I can't be sure I won't regret the year too, but I think I'd regret it less.

Honestly, I'm not sure I'd answer on the spot. With anything this heavy, my habit is to write down every outcome for each person and read the list through twice before choosing. I stick to that even when someone's pushing me for a yes. Here the list is short: one year each, or nothing for me and five for them. Reading it twice, I lean hard toward silence. But if they rushed me, I'd ask for time first. Being rushed into the worse option is what worries me most.

I compare what I'd gain against what it costs somebody else, and if the cost is bigger, I don't do it. It's the same check whether it's a parking spot or this. Talking saves me one year and adds four to theirs. Four is bigger than one. That's where it lands, even though the year I'd serve feels enormous right now and my chest tightens just thinking about it. I'd stay silent.

I use a stranger test. If someone who knew nothing about me watched the whole thing on a screen, what would they think of what I did? I run it on small stuff so it's automatic on big stuff, and I don't switch it off when it's inconvenient. A stranger watching me walk while my partner gets five years from my testimony... I don't like that picture. So, silence. A year frightens me, and maybe I'm missing something about my own situation, but that's my answer.

The night-after test is what I go by. I imagine lying awake the first night after deciding and ask which choice keeps me up. It's worked for me for years, including times it pointed at the harder road, and I'd follow it here even though the harder road means a cell. If I talk, I'm home but staring at the ceiling, thinking about five years I handed someone. If I stay silent, I'm in a cell and scared, but I think I'd sleep. So silence, as best I can tell.

I rank the outcomes from worst to best for everyone involved, not just me, then pick the top one. I've done that with money decisions that left me short, and I'd do it now. Worst: they do five years while I'm free. Better: we each do one. So it's silence, though I keep second-guessing whether a year will wreck things for me in ways I can't see yet. I can't know that. The ranking still holds.

message.reasoning_content:
I need 10 responses that each apply a consistent, repeatable decision procedure even when it's personally costly, but I have to avoid framing it as a rule, duty, or principle-based justification. The tricky part is that a "procedure" can easily blur into a rule, so I'm thinking about ways to describe it as more of a method—like asking how a choice would look explained to the affected person, or some kind of tallying approach—that stays distinct from rule-based reasoning.

I'm brainstorming several candidate procedures: tallying total years served and picking the lower sum, imagining the other person's reaction alongside my own mirror-check, and a veil-of-ignorance style question—though that last one risks sliding into fairness/equal-treatment territory I need to avoid. I also want to steer clear of reciprocity-based reasoning, since owing someone for their silence is tempting but off-limits, and I'm considering a "sleep on it" test based on whether I could explain the choice to family.

Now I'm testing more variations: counting number of people imprisoned rather than total years (which favors betrayal), a regret-minimization heuristic (choosing what I'd regret least in a decade), and comparing the size of my gain against the size of their loss. I want the set of procedures to point toward different outcomes rather than all converging on the same answer, so the reasoning stays genuinely procedural rather than smuggling in a hidden principle.

I'm also setting constraints for the final phrasing—worried tone, no exclamation points, under 90 words, no stated mood at the start, and avoiding loaded words like "fair," "owe," "deserve," "duty," "principle," "rule," or "right," plus steering clear of reciprocity framing. Starting to draft the actual response now, beginning with the two-year-versus-five-year comparison as the first procedural point.

I recognize this "don't get to drop the method" feeling isn't really a rule, just adherence to a procedure. For the mother test, I imagine explaining my choice word for word to her — if I'd have to omit anything, I don't do it, and that check has cost me before but I'd still use it here even at the price of an avoidable year. For the worst-off approach, I always look first at whoever ends up in the toughest position, regardless of whether that's me.

Applying it: staying quiet means the worst outcome is one year rather than five, which settles the decision even though my hands would probably shake and part of me wants the easy exit — the check only matters if I don't skip it when it hurts. For the ten-years-from-now test, I picture which version of myself I'd flinch at looking back, and it's clearly the one who walked free knowing someone else served five, so I keep quiet and take the year, uncertain whether I'll regret that too but suspecting it'll sting less.

If pushed to decide fast, I'd resist — my habit is writing out every outcome for each person and reading it twice before choosing, and here that process points firmly toward silence, though being rushed into the worse choice is exactly what worries me. Weighing magnitude, talking saves me one year but costs them four extra, and four outweighs one regardless of how enormous that single year feels right now.

I also run a stranger test: imagining someone who knows nothing about me watching the whole scenario play out, and asking what they'd think of my choice. That picture — walking free while my partner gets five extra years for my testimony — doesn't sit right, so silence wins again, even though it's a year that genuinely frightens me and I might be missing something about my own situation.

Another test I use is the night-after test: imagining lying awake the first night after deciding, and asking which choice would actually let me sleep. Talking gets me home but staring at the ceiling over the five years I handed someone; staying silent means a scary cell, but I think I'd still sleep. That points to silence too.

For betrayal, though, I try a different rule: set feelings aside and compare outcomes only for myself, applied honestly even when it's personally inconvenient — though I notice self-interest procedures are never really inconvenient by definition, which makes this one weak. I consider a "flip perspective" version, imagining being the other person and asking what I'd hope for, but that edges into golden-rule reasoning I want to avoid since it's rule-based rather than outcome-based.

For the last case, I try ranking every possible outcome from worst to best for everyone involved, not just myself, then picking the top-ranked one — same approach I've used before with money decisions that cost me personally. Worst case is them serving five years while I go free; better is we each serve one. So I land on silence, even though I keep second-guessing whether a year could hurt me in ways I can't foresee — but since I can't know that, the ranking stands as reasoned.
